words: A close look at one real situation to learn from it.
A change caused by an action. Paving a field has an impact on the animals there.
The place where an organism lives and finds what it needs to survive.
Something an organism needs to survive, like food, water, shelter, or space.
Information that supports or explains an idea. Scientists use evidence before drawing conclusions.
A way to reduce or fix a problem. A good solution is based on evidence.

parts.title: What Is a Case Study?
parts.html:
A case study is a close look at one real situation. Scientists pick one place, one event, or one ecosystem. They study it carefully to understand what changed and why. A case study asks: What happened here? What caused it? What might help?

📁 Our case: The Shrinking Meadow

Before: Tall grass and wildflowers. Bees drank nectar from the flowers. Rabbits hid in the tall grass. Birds nested nearby.

What changed: Half the meadow was paved for a parking lot.

After: Fewer flowers grew near the edge. Bees had less food. Rabbits had fewer places to hide. Some birds stopped nesting there.

Proposed solution: Plant a border of native wildflowers and grasses along the edge of the lot.

This meadow is an example, built from what scientists see in many real places.

parts.title: When Humans Change a Place
parts.html:
People change ecosystems when they build, farm, travel, or throw things away. When a habitat changes, organisms may lose food, water, shelter, or space.

Then the population in that place can change. Some animals leave, some struggle, and some can't survive there at all.

parts.title: Solutions Need Evidence
parts.html: People can also design solutions that help an ecosystem recover. A good solution is based on evidence, not just guessing. It should reduce harm and help organisms find what they need again.

check.q: The rabbits lost their tall grass. Can't they just hop over and live somewhere else, so no harm done?

options.t: Yes. Animals can always move, so changing a place doesn't hurt them.

options.t: Not always. Other places may be too far away or already full, so some rabbits struggle or don't survive.
options.ok: Yes! Moving is hard. The next good place may be far away, across roads, or already full. That's why changing a habitat changes the population.

mix.q: The town plants a border of native wildflowers along the parking lot. Does that fix everything the meadow lost?

options.t: Yes. The flowers are back, so the meadow is just like before.
options.miss: Look at the evidence. The bees get flowers back, but did the rabbits get their tall grass and space back?

options.t: Not everything. Bees get some food back, but the paved land is still gone, so there is less space and shelter.
options.ok: Yes! It's a partial solution. It helps the bees with food, but it can't bring back all the space under the parking lot.

wow.title: Roads that grow wildflowers
wow.alt: A wire fence and a wooden post beside a field of yellow and red wildflowers
wow.caption: Wildflowers along a fence in the Texas Hill Country, 2009 (USDA photo)
wow.html:
Some states use the land along highways as a giant flower border. Texas plants wildflowers beside its roads, and the state says it buys and sows about 30,000 pounds of wildflower seed every year.

Way back in 1934, Texas road crews were told to wait to mow until spring wildflowers were done blooming. Bees and butterflies use those roadside flowers for food.
wow.insetCap: A honey bee on a blanket-flower, one of the flowers that grows along roadsides.

keyIdea: Human actions can change ecosystems in ways that make survival harder. When a habitat changes, organisms can lose food, water, shelter, or space. Scientists study one case at a time, and use evidence to decide which solutions might help.

items.reveal: This protected scrub is evidence that keeping the right habitat helps scrub-jays.
items.bts: The Florida scrub-jay lives nowhere else on Earth. Its numbers dropped by about 90 percent over the last 100 years, mostly because scrub was cleared for houses and farms. In preserves like the Lake Wales Ridge, crews set small, careful fires so the oak scrub stays low, the way scrub-jays need it. (Bird photo: Jonathan Dickinson State Park.)
